# Inksheaf — design critique

## 1. What the images actually show

**Strengths.** The material vocabulary is working. The engraved sheaf (Images 1, 3, 6) is the best asset in the set: a single incised mark, no gloss, no gradient — it earns the "burned into the wood" brief. The lamp falloff in Image 1 is believable. Type voice is restrained and consistent: transitional serif headline, italic single-line subhead, brick-red letterspaced small-caps label. Image 4 is the most credible screen you have, because it says real things: 22 essays, 179 estimated pages, a date range, an itemized price, "Nothing prints until you approve your proof. Readers order from Lulu," and an honest note that one archive post is excluded. That paragraph does more for trust than the whole desk scene.

**Visible faults, hero (Images 1–3).** The owner's objection is legible in the pixels. In Image 1 the headline, label, input and button are frontal, axis-aligned HTML sitting on a page that recedes to the right — two incompatible geometries in one rectangle. Each page reads roughly square rather than 6×9. The left page is 100% empty, so half the composition is dead. The book bleeds off the right frame edge and the lower-left board has no cris
message.reasoning:
I'm planning a concise critique covering five sections, starting by examining the desktop hero image closely. The book spread shows a blank left page and flat frontal text sitting awkwardly on a receding page plane, with proportions that look too wide and short for a proper 6×9 book.

Continuing the desktop analysis, I notice the book's corner floats without a proper contact shadow, it bleeds off the frame edge, and there's a stray lamp pull chain near the logo. The underline input field has low contrast against the gradient, and the header duplicates the primary CTA — though the palette, serif typeface, and engraved sheaf all work well.

Now looking at the mobile version, the book crops down to an unreadable beige panel with no visible spine or pages, the cover shows an odd rounded corner at top, the lamp base reads as an unrecognizable brass blob, and the sheaf engraving sits awkwardly off-center at the bottom.

Then examining the angled correction draft, I see the skewed text becomes nearly illegible, red rectangles overlap the publication label looking like validation errors, the book takes on a floppy, oddly bulging shape with a folded spine, and there's no contact shadow beneath the left board — confirming this approach should be rejected. Finally checking the desktop preview, the essay count, page count, date range, pricing, and approval messaging are strong, though the cover thumbnail itself looks problematic.

Image 5 (mobile look-inside) shows the same identity bug with byline "CAITHRIN" instead of the publication name, and no Substack logo. The page renders as a bare table of contents with five post titles and no folio or body text, framed in a double gold border that competes with the inner card's own rounded corners and shadow — two containers fighting each other — plus a mis-rendered arrow glyph next to "Back to the cover."

For image 6, I'm measuring the spread proportions directly from pixel coordinates: each page comes out to roughly 550×740px, giving an aspect ratio near 0.74 versus the target 6×9 ratio of 0.667, meaning the pages read as noticeably too wide and squat and need narrowing by about 10%.

The gutter itself also looks off — the pages meet in an almost flat, straight seam with no real curvature or shadow, which reads more like a lay-flat notebook than a perfect-bound book, since perfect binding shouldn't allow the spread to lie this flat. I'm also noting the right page appears wider than the left, and the top edges of the two pages don't quite align vertically.

The contact shadow between the book and the wood surface is weak, giving it a pasted-on look rather than sitting naturally on the desk, and there's no visible page-block thickness despite the claimed page count, so it reads as a thin sketchbook instead. The engraved sheaf brand is legible top-down, but the implied light direction in its shading doesn't quite match the lamp's position at upper-left.

The brand mark also sits in the left margin where mobile cropping would cut it off, and it's scaled too large relative to the book, competing visually with the Inksheaf wordmark rather than complementing it. On the positive side, the two blank pages give clean rectangular areas of usable, in-plane text space, meaning real HTML text could sit crisply and remain selectable without perspective distortion — though the lamp base is awkwardly cropped into an anonymous brass ring.

Before implementation I need to fix several things: correct the page aspect ratio to 2:3, add a believable gutter shadow and page bow near the spine (or better, switch to a single recto page to avoid the lay-flat illusion problem), add occlusion shadow and visible page-block thickness, shrink the engraving and keep it outside the text-safe zone, and regenerate the image at 2x as a background plate with a defined safe rectangle and solid-color fallback so text doesn't depend on the image loading. For the actual composition, I'm leaning toward a static desktop background with no parallax or scroll-driven camera, using a two-column layout with the headline occupying roughly the left 44%.

Right side holds the overhead plate cropped to a single recto page at true 2:3 for the preview. Actually simpler: I'll put the headline, input, and button as normal HTML on the desk surface rather than on the paper itself, keeping the book purely for content — this sidesteps the "text in wrong plane" issue and the awkwardness of UI rendered on paper. On submit, instead of moving the camera, the page cross-fades in place to an identity card showing the publication's logo, name, handle, essay count, page count, date range, and price, with two buttons: "Read a sample page" and "Reserve this print run" — the former swapping in a real typeset page.

For the sample page itself, I want the running head to be the actual title, real opening text from a genuine post, a real folio, and a caption outside the paper clarifying that pagination is set per proof, so nothing invented masquerades as real. I'll add prev/next buttons that are tab-focusable, keep scroll native, and size the hero to fit under 100vh so the input never requires scrolling.

For mobile, I'm dropping the desk photo to a thin band or full-bleed dark walnut background without the book, putting headline and input first at full width with 16px+ inputs to avoid iOS zoom, then a single upright 2:3 page card below with swipe/prev-next navigation instead of an unreadable spread.

Now I'm sketching four distinct visual directions for the publication, framed as proposals covering typography, palette, logo, and hierarchy. The first is a "Quarterly" editorial letterpress direction: a transitional serif title, small caps subtitle, colophon rules, warm oat/oxblood/ink-black palette, a blind-debossed monochrome logo device, and a single-column interior with alternating running heads between publication title and essay title.

The second is a "Field notebook" utilitarian modern direction: a humanist sans with wide letterspaced caps, a slate blue-grey and warm white palette with a signal orange accent, a small top-left badge logo, a huge left-aligned stacked title with no ornament, and an interior mixing serif text with sans running heads, marginal date stamps, and metadata at each essay head.

The third direction, "Archive/library" scholarly classicism, is starting to take shape with an old-style serif, true italics, roman numeral volume markers, and a deep forest or oxblood cover with a cream label panel and gold accents.

I need presets to actually map to the print renderer, with a "sample page reflects the selected preset" behavior, and fonts should be excluded if they can't be licensed for print.

For acceptance checks, I'm listing what screenshots can't prove: identity needs to resolve correctly across five publications including edge cases like missing logos or unicode titles, since a screenshot only captures one moment, not the resolver's behavior across accounts or cache states. Sample page authenticity requires real body text from an actual post with correct byline, with every non-final element clearly labeled outside the page area.

Input reachability needs to work at both mobile and desktop viewports with proper tab order and visible focus rings, none of which a screenshot can verify. Motion and scroll behavior must respect reduced-motion preferences, avoid scroll hijacking, and show no layout shift—claims that can't come from stills. Finally, geometry and asset integrity require the page plate to be exactly 2:3 with a defined safe text rect and fallback handling for failed images, with no stray artifacts.

Print fidelity concerns like trim, bleed, and gutter creep across 179 pages need an actual proof PDF, not a screenshot. Given the roughly 1200-word budget, I should write this tightly.
